correctness.rationale: The graph is the simple orientation-forgetting Kautz graph on ordered unequal pairs; the signatures are open-neighborhood intersections, and only outsiders are compared. I checked the monotonicity proof by restriction of larger-set signatures to the smaller set. An independent clause-branching calculation encoded coverage by {v} ∪ N(v) and outsider separation by {u,v} ∪ (N(u) △ N(v)); a set satisfies every clause exactly when it is locating-dominating. At a chosen unhit clause, branching on the least ultimately selected available member partitions all feasible extensions; supersets of smaller clauses are redundant. Every accepted set was also checked against its actual signatures. Exact k−1 counts were zero; exact minimum triples (k, labeled, natural orbits) were (1,2,1), (3,20,3), (4,168,7), (5,84,2), (7,11040,16), (8,13860,5). Attaining sets from all six rows were checked separately. Generator closure under adjacent alphabet transpositions and reversal gives the full stated histograms, including size:multiplicity 120:2,360:4,720:7,1440:3 and 630:2,2520:1,5040:2. value.rationale: The minimum number of sensors needed to distinguish all unsensored vertices is a natural input to network identification. The first failure of the q-sensor budget and the distinct symmetry types of optimal layouts give exact design benchmarks; this is more than one isolated candidate or a repetition of all-vertex code counts. The value is finite and graph-theoretic, not a claim about larger alphabets or physical sensing.
